book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook gives the two definitions side by side and a table of differences. Here the video offers the common definition (rising GDP), breaks it with a made-up country whose population outruns GDP, repairs it (per capita income), breaks it again with a second made-up fact (poverty rises, literacy falls), asks 'why?', answers by following where the money was spent, and only then names development. The history (trickle-down and its failure) comes after the concept, as the story of how economists learned the same lesson; a cliff-hanger on measuring development closes it.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each candidate definition is tested on a small made-up country; when its numbers break the definition, the fix becomes the next teachable piece.

opening.what: Every country has a national income measured as GDP, NDP, GNP or NNP, and GDP is the one used to compare countries; flags sit over an empty national-income band.

moves.concept: national income measures (GDP, NDP, GNP, NNP)
moves.what: Recalls the four measures and that GDP is used to compare economies.

moves.concept: first guess: growth = rising GDP
moves.what: If we draw a country's GDP graph and see a stretch where it keeps rising, some economists call it a period of economic growth.

moves.concept: first guess: growth = rising GDP
moves.what: But is it right to define growth this way?

moves.concept: counter-example: GDP up, population up faster, per capita income down
moves.what: Chaliye, let us see with an example.

moves.concept: counter-example: GDP up, population up faster, per capita income down
moves.what: GDP goes from 10 lakh to 50 lakh, but population goes from 1,000 to 10,000.

moves.concept: counter-example: GDP up, population up faster, per capita income down
moves.what: So per capita income falls from 1,000 to 500.

moves.concept: counter-example: GDP up, population up faster, per capita income down
moves.what: GDP growth was positive, lekin population grew faster than GDP, so per capita income fell.

moves.concept: counter-example: GDP up, population up faster, per capita income down
moves.what: Most economists say such a period cannot be called economic growth at all.

moves.concept: growth = sustained rise in per capita income
moves.what: So one thing is clear: the graph should be drawn for per capita income.

moves.concept: growth = sustained rise in per capita income
moves.what: On a per capita graph, a stretch where per capita income keeps rising is a period of economic growth, and economists agree.

moves.concept: growth = sustained rise in per capita income
moves.what: Gives the period made-up years: it starts in 2020 and peaks in 2024.

moves.concept: growth without benefit: poverty up, literacy down
moves.what: 'If I share more information': people below the poverty line went from 10% to 15%, and literacy from 45% to 30%.

moves.concept: growth without benefit: poverty up, literacy down
moves.what: Did this growth benefit all the people? No. Then the big question: how can a country grow and its people not benefit?

moves.concept: why: income not spent on health and education
moves.what: Growth raises national income, but if none of it goes to healthcare or education and all goes to defence, people's quality of life does not improve.

moves.concept: economic development = quality of life
moves.what: Economists call this quality of life economic development (named after the problem was felt).

moves.concept: history: interchangeable terms, trickle-down theory, its failure, the 1970s distinction
moves.what: Before 1960 the two terms were used as one; after the 1960s data showed countries, especially in the Gulf, with fast growth but low quality of life.

moves.concept: history: interchangeable terms, trickle-down theory, its failure, the 1970s distinction
moves.what: The popular trickle-down theory said growth would lift quality of life by itself, so focus only on growth.

moves.concept: history: interchangeable terms, trickle-down theory, its failure, the 1970s distinction
moves.what: But in the 1960s the results showed the theory failing.

moves.concept: history: interchangeable terms, trickle-down theory, its failure, the 1970s distinction
moves.what: In the 1970s a Pakistani economist, Mahbub ul Haq, first spelled out the difference between growth and development.

moves.concept: growth is necessary but not sufficient for development
moves.what: 'But don't forget': guards against swinging too far; a country must first achieve growth to reach development.

moves.concept: growth is necessary but not sufficient for development
moves.what: Development (better quality of life) needs money, and money comes from growth.

moves.concept: growth is necessary but not sufficient for development
moves.what: Growth is needed for development, but growth does not bring development automatically.

moves.concept: growth has measures; how to measure development is open
moves.what: Growth can be measured many ways, but how do we measure quality of life? A hard question economists took 10-15 years to answer.

moves.concept: growth has measures; how to measure development is open
moves.what: You will get the answer in the next video (cliff-hanger).

examples.what: GDP 10 lakh to 50 lakh while population goes 1,000 to 10,000, so per capita income falls 1,000 to 500.

examples.carries: rising per capita income can coexist with worse lives

examples.what: The growth money goes entirely to defence, none to health or education.
examples.carries: why growth may not improve quality of life (development)

examples.what: Countries, especially in the Gulf, with fast growth but low quality of life (as the video states).
examples.carries: why economists separated the two terms

examples.what: The trickle-down theory's promise and its failure on the evidence.
examples.carries: the history of the growth-development distinction

narration.density: About eight key terms (national income measures, economic growth, per capita income, below poverty line, literacy rate, quality of life, economic development, trickle-down theory) in about 325 s, about 1.5 per minute. Comfortable: numbers and questions carry most of the time, so the pace suits a first look at the topic.

talmel_summary: The picture usually runs 1-5 s ahead of the voice: labels, notes and a new axis appear before they are spoken. That works for the counter-examples, because each number sits on the chart where the eye can check it before the voice concludes. The strongest fits show the step: drop lines from GDP points to population, the axis swap to per capita, the crossed benefit arrow with spending branches, the staircase and the empty measuring tape. Weak: notes that copy the speech (interchangeable, trickle-down claim), and information only on screen (government as spender, 138 crore).

voice.notes: About 190 words per minute, friendly and quick. Uses first-person framing to bring in new facts ('agar main aapse kuch aur information share karoon'), then turns them into questions to the viewer and answers them ('to iska answer hoga: nahi'). Large numbers are read in Indian units (10 lakh, 50 lakh); percentages plainly. The 'but don't forget' line near the end is said more firmly than the rest. No long pauses.

game_ideas.player_does: Runs a small country year by year with two sliders: GDP growth and population growth.
game_ideas.process_happens: Two lines draw: GDP and per capita income; a stretch is labelled PERIOD OF ECONOMIC GROWTH only while per capita income keeps rising.
game_ideas.win: Produce five years of sustained per capita growth.
game_ideas.lose: Raising GDP while population grows faster makes per capita income fall; the growth title turns pink and gets a red cross, as in the video.
game_ideas.concept: growth = sustained rise in per capita income

game_ideas.player_does: As the government, splits each year's extra national income among healthcare, education and defence.
game_ideas.process_happens: The crowd's below-poverty-line and literacy meters respond; the benefit arrow from the growth card reaches the crowd only when health and education get enough.
game_ideas.win: Growth years that also show poverty falling and literacy rising: the staircase figure steps up to DEVELOPMENT.
game_ideas.lose: Putting it all into defence keeps growth on but crosses the benefit arrow and worsens the meters, showing growth without development.

game_ideas.player_does: Orders cards: terms used as one before 1960, trickle-down theory popular, 1960s data of high growth with low quality of life, theory fails, 1970s distinction, the open question of measuring development.
game_ideas.process_happens: Each placed card adds its piece to the timeline picture (note, theory line, crossed arrow, staircase, empty tape).
game_ideas.win: Timeline complete with the empty measuring tape at the end.
game_ideas.lose: Putting the 1970s distinction before the failure shows nothing yet to disprove, with a nudge to place the evidence first.

checks_learned: Made-up country figures must carry an on-screen 'example, not reality' note while they are shown (E35 does this; enforce it everywhere).
Every number shown on screen (138 crore) should be spoken, or dropped.
An actor the picture adds (the government as spender) must also be named by the voice.
When the voice rejects a definition, the screen must visibly strike it (the red cross on the growth title worked; enforce it).
A derived value (per capita = GDP / population) should show its division step on screen, not only the results.
Notes that repeat the narration should not appear more than about 3 s before the voice reaches them.
A cliff-hanger close must still recap what was settled before opening the next question.

teaching_best.why: The common definition is broken by four small numbers drawn on the same chart: GDP up fivefold, people up tenfold, per head halved.
The fix is shown by swapping only the y-axis to per capita income, so the learner sees exactly what changed in the definition.
A benefit arrow crossed before the crowd, then a government node with health and education crossed and defence ticked, answers 'why?' by following the money.
The two-step staircase makes 'necessary but not sufficient' a picture, and the empty measuring tape sets up the next lesson.

teaching_weak.why: Flags over an empty band carry little meaning for the recall.
The history runs on small text notes and a tiny country table; the Gulf example is spoken but not shown.
A real photo and a note carry the economist; the voice gives no idea of what he proposed beyond 'the difference'.
Per capita income values appear without showing how they were worked out (division by population is never stated).
